definition: The Klee–Minty cube or Klee–Minty polytope (named after Victor Klee and George J.
details: Minty) is a unit hypercube of variable dimension whose corners have been perturbed. Klee and Minty demonstrated that George Dantzig's simplex algorithm has poor worst-case performance when initialized at one corner of their "squashed cube". On the three-dimensional version, the simplex algorithm and the criss-cross algorithm visit all 8 corners in the worst case. In particular, many optimization algorithms for linear optimization exhibit poor performance when applied to the Klee–Minty cube. In 1973 Klee and Minty showed that Dantzig's simplex algorithm was not a polynomial-time algorithm when applied to their cube. Later, modifications of the Klee–Minty cube have shown poor behavior both for other basis-exchange pivoting algorithms and also for interior-point algorithms.

explainer.lead: The Klee–Minty cube is a deliberately distorted cube that exposes how badly some optimization methods can behave in the worst case. It matters because an algorithm that usually works quickly can still be forced to take an extremely long route before finding the answer.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a treasure hunt inside a squashed box where the fastest-looking move keeps sending you to another corner instead of the treasure. This special box can make a solver visit every corner before finishing. It shows that a usually speedy method can still have a surprisingly bad day.
tiers.practitioner: The Klee–Minty cube is used to analyze worst-case behavior in linear optimization rather than as a routine performance benchmark. It is a reminder not to infer polynomial-time guarantees from the simplex algorithm’s practical speed, and related constructions also challenge other pivoting and interior-point methods.
tiers.paperLevel: The Klee–Minty polytope is a variable-dimensional unit hypercube whose corners have been perturbed. Klee and Minty showed in 1973 that Dantzig’s simplex algorithm, initialized at a designated corner, is not polynomial-time on this construction. In three dimensions, both the simplex and criss-cross algorithms visit all eight corners in the worst case; modifications also produce poor behavior for other basis-exchange and interior-point algorithms.

explainer.example: On the three-dimensional Klee–Minty cube, the simplex algorithm can visit all 8 corners in the worst case. The criss-cross algorithm can also visit all 8 corners on this version.

explainer.intuition: A small distortion of a cube can steer an optimization algorithm into visiting corner after corner before reaching its goal. The construction separates typical practical speed from worst-case guarantees.
howItWorks: Start with a unit hypercube of chosen dimension.
Perturb its corners to create the squashed Klee–Minty polytope.
Initialize the simplex algorithm at the designated corner.
Follow its pivots along a path that can visit every corner.
Use the resulting path length to expose poor worst-case performance.
explainer.whyItMatters: Klee and Minty’s 1973 result disproved the idea that Dantzig’s simplex algorithm was polynomial-time on their construction. It remains a clear warning that strong everyday performance does not guarantee a good worst-case bound.
misconceptions: It does not show that every linear program is hard for the simplex algorithm.
It does not mean the simplex algorithm is always slow in practice.
Its worst-case behavior is not limited to a three-dimensional cube.
